title: What's the weather like?
paragraphs: My name is Aizat Sarsenova. I am nineteen years old and I come from Astana — the capital city of Kazakhstan. I study Ecology at WKU in Uralsk. It is my first year here, and one of the biggest surprises has been the weather. Before I moved to Uralsk, my friends in Astana warned me: "The weather in the west is different. Be ready." They were absolutely right — but not in the way I expected.

Astana is famous for its extreme weather. In winter, the temperature drops to minus thirty degrees or even lower. The wind there is sharp, dry, and relentless — it comes across the open steppe with nothing to stop it. Snowstorms are common. On the coldest days, the sky is a bright, sharp blue, the air is completely clear, and the streets are empty because nobody wants to go outside. It is beautiful in a harsh, dramatic way — but it is also genuinely dangerous if you are not dressed properly.

When I arrived in Uralsk in September, the weather was mild and surprisingly warm. The sky was a soft, pale blue with a few white clouds. The air smelt of dry grass and autumn leaves. I walked from the dormitory to the main building without a coat — something I would never do in Astana at that time of year. The temperature was around eighteen degrees. It felt almost like summer to me.

October brought the first real change. The sky turned grey and heavy. Rain fell every few days — light, quiet rain, the kind that soaks you slowly without you realising. The temperature dropped to around eight or ten degrees. I started wearing my thick green jumper and my waterproof jacket. The trees in the university courtyard turned orange and red. It was a beautiful season — wet, golden, and melancholy all at the same time.

By November, winter had arrived properly. The first snow fell on a Tuesday morning — light, dry flakes that covered the ground in just a few hours. The temperature was minus five degrees. I wrapped a long woollen scarf around my neck, put on my warmest boots, and wore two layers under my coat. But even then, the wind was cold and sharp against my face. Uralsk in winter is not as extreme as Astana, but it is still serious. You need good clothes to survive it.

My favourite weather, I have discovered, is early spring — March or April, when the snow begins to melt and the temperature rises to five or six degrees above zero. Everything feels lighter. The sky is a clean, bright blue. There is still frost on the ground in the mornings, but by noon the sun is warm and pleasant. In those moments, walking between lectures, I feel happy to be a student in Uralsk — even if the winters are long and the wind is cold.

dialogue.speaker: Ruslan
dialogue.text: Aizat! You look frozen. How cold is it outside right now?

dialogue.speaker: Aizat
dialogue.text: Minus eight degrees and very windy! I cannot feel my nose anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Ruslan
dialogue.text: Is it colder than Astana? I thought Astana was the coldest city in Kazakhstan.

dialogue.speaker: Aizat
dialogue.text: Astana is colder in winter — minus thirty sometimes! But the wind here is terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Ruslan
dialogue.text: What was the weather like when you first arrived in September?

dialogue.speaker: Aizat
dialogue.text: Warm and mild — about eighteen degrees! I walked without a coat. It was wonderful.

dialogue.speaker: Ruslan
dialogue.text: And now? How do you find the Uralsk winter compared to home?

dialogue.speaker: Aizat
dialogue.text: Less extreme, but still serious. The wind is very sharp and cold here.

dialogue.speaker: Aizat
dialogue.text: Early spring — March and April. The sky is clean blue and the sun is warm at noon.

dialogue.speaker: Ruslan
dialogue.text: What does the weather forecast say for this week?

dialogue.speaker: Aizat
dialogue.text: Snow on Thursday and Friday — and minus twelve by the weekend. Wear your warmest coat!
